lines: When a hurricane makes landfall, recovery funding can only move as fast as the damage is documented.
Today, that means inspectors walking site after site, measuring by hand, and building each federal damage record one line at a time.
It's slow, it's expensive, and it's where recovery stalls.
Now picture one connected workflow, from a drone in the air to a finished damage record.
It starts with flight. A wide sweep maps the entire community within hours.
Then detailed flights capture each priority facility from every angle, with survey-grade positioning.
Imagery lands in a secure cloud environment, checked and catalogued with a full chain of custody.
There, it's stitched into a seamless map and a three-dimensional surface model.
Next, the models learn from experts, not from scratch.
We start from an open Texas A and M dataset of more than twenty-one thousand labelled buildings.
In Roboflow, a plain-language prompt drafts new labels, and an AI agent runs the job.
Specialists correct what it misses, and we train two models: one for the whole community, and one for each building.
Then the models go to work.
Every building gets a damage rating, every road a status, and response teams get a route around what's blocked.
This is real labelled data, from Fort Myers Beach after Hurricane Ian.
At each priority facility, the system pinpoints every defect, measures it, and records exactly how certain it is.
People stay in control. Analysts confirm, reject, or send each finding to the field.
And every correction makes the next model sharper.
Confirmed findings flow into the Damage Description and Dimensions, the FEMA record the inspector verifies.
The client receives the complete package: maps, measurements, imagery, and the evidence behind every line.
One workflow. From flight, to field, to funding.
The pieces exist today. Connecting them is the opportunity.
